255 PM EDT Fri Oct 9 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 254 PM EDT Friday...

Rainfall amounts on Sunday have increased slightly with most 
locations seeing between a quarter to half of an inch of rain with 
closer to a tenth of an inch of rain near the Canadian Border.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 254 PM EDT Friday...

1. Showers end this afternoon with drier weather expected 
through Sunday afternoon. Rainfall associated with the remnants of 
Hurricane Isaias will impact the region Sunday evening and overnight 
but not flooding is expected.

2. Widespread showers are expected on Tuesday ahead of a 
seasonably strong frontal system, leading to sharply cooler and 
drier weather for Wednesday into Thursday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 254 PM EDT Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: We continue to be under the influence of an upper level 
trough with a pocket of cold air aloft. This has lead to convective 
showers once again which should taper off this evening with the loss 
of daytime heating and building mid-level heights and increasing 
subsidence. Deep layer ridging will then begin to build into the 
region overnight with Saturday looking to be a beautiful but chilly 
day with plenty of sunshine, light winds, and highs in the mid 50s. 
This ridge will remain entrenched across the North Country through 
Sunday morning before the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will shunt 
the ridge eastward. Widespread rainfall will hold off until after 
sunset on Sunday for most locations with a quarter to half of an 
inch of rain expected for many locations. Areas near the Canadian 
Border will likely see the least rainfall with amounts closer to a 
tenth of an inch. The RRFS and NAM are hinting at a pocket of 
frontogenetic forcing in the northwest sector of the remnants Sunday 
night and are beginning to show a pocket of enhanced rain totals 
nearing 1.5 inches. This will likely change run to run and with the 
lack of mesoscale models having the temporal resolution to analyze 
this feature, we won't know about placement of this possible banded 
precipitation until tomorrow afternoon most likely. Nevertheless, 
the rainfall seen Sunday night, even if it's in the 1-1.5 inch rain 
locally, will be highly beneficial with no flood concerns 
anticipated at this time. A strengthening mid-level jet Sunday night 
will act to quickly shift these remnants eastward with dry 
conditions expected by daybreak on Monday.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Following the rain on Sunday night, another high 
probability rainfall event (about 100% chance of rain) is setting up 
for Tuesday. It appears moisture from the remnants of Tropical Storm 
Rachel in the eastern Pacific gets pushed into a strengthening front 
approaching from the north. An associated jet streak situated to our 
northeast will help increase large scale lift such that rain becomes 
widespread ahead of the boundary beginning early Tuesday morning. 
Would expect numerous showers and even a chance of thunder (around 
10% is too low to mention in the forecast) with some elevated 
instability likely. The temperature forecast for Tuesday given the 
position of the thermally strong cold front is rather uncertain. 
However, very moist low level air will limit temperatures even in 
the warm side of the boundary. Meanwhile, shallow cold air advection 
is noted in forecast soundings, such that areas such as the northern 
St. Lawrence Valley could see temperatures fall into the 40s during 
the day. 

Currently, probabilities of rainfall in excess of 1" during this 
event are mainly 20-45% and trend a bit higher towards northernmost 
New York and Vermont. For 0.5" these probabilities are about 40-70%. 
The evolution of this system Tuesday afternoon/evening is actually 
fairly uncertain, with one cluster of guidance favoring a faster 
exit and others keeping rain in the area through Tuesday night. It 
appears the front will finally clear the region as low pressure 
deepens to our east by Wednesday morning, in what could be a long 
duration rainfall event. Perhaps there will be enough moisture for 
some early season upslope mountain snow showers Tuesday night/early 
Wednesday if the cold air advection is sufficiently strong. 
Otherwise, while there is some spread in the upper air pattern for 
the remainder of next week, overall the consensus right now is for 
seasonably cool and breezy conditions on Wednesday ahead of a ridge 
of high pressure that preserves dry weather through at least 
Thursday.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z FRIDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Through 18Z Saturday...A large cluster of showers in eastern Ontario
is moving towards the airspace, with high probabilities of producing
rain over the course of about 30 to 90 minutes at most terminals.
Within those showers, there will likely be some MVFR intervals due
to visibility primarily, and have used TEMPO groups at terminals
where chances are greatest. Most of this activity will move through
in the 20Z to 00Z timeframe, peaking in the 21-23Z range based on
radar trends. Westerly winds in and outside of showers could
occasionally gust in the 15 to 25 knot range through the next six
hours, trending northwesterly. Winds after 00Z will become lighter,
and possibly calm especially in New York sites as high pressure
builds in from the west. Think MSS may see fog development with
combination of recent rain and light flow, with greater confidence
in the 09Z to 11Z period. There are some hints at fog at SLK as well
and have mention of BR after 08Z for now, but could see some fog
earlier especially with more evening rainfall. Otherwise, mainly VFR
conditions are expected.

Outlook...

Saturday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Sunday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Columbus Day: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Monday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Likely SHRA.
Tuesday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Likely SHRA.
Tuesday Night: Mainly MVFR, with areas IFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Wednesday: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. NO SIG WX.
